questions.subject: MATH
questions.topic: Counting principles: sum and product rules
questions.learningObjective: Solve problems involving counting principles: sum and product rules.
questions.stem: In this exercise, exactly how many strings of length 4 can be formed from an character set of 6 symbols if repetition is allowed?

options.misconception: Wrong belief "forbids repetition without justification" gives 360, not 1296.
Wrong belief "swaps the string length and alphabet size" gives 4096, not 1296.
Wrong belief "omits one valid string" gives 1295, not 1296.

questions.explanation: Each of the 4 positions can be filled independently by any of the 6 symbols, so by the product rule there are 6 to the power 4, namely 1296, strings.
questions.hint: Every position has the same number of independent choices.

provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.learningObjective: Solve problems involving permutations and arrangements.
questions.stem: In how many ways can 10 distinct books be arranged in a row on a shelf?

options.misconception: Wrong belief "fixes one book for no reason" gives 362880, not 3628800.
Wrong belief "uses a quadratic instead of a factorial" gives 100, not 3628800.
Wrong belief "arranges only two of the books" gives 90, not 3628800.

questions.explanation: Arranging 10 distinct objects in a line is a permutation of all of them, giving 10 factorial which equals 3628800.
questions.hint: Count every ordering of the distinct objects.
